entries.answer: Let's Match (lets-match.com) is a live web app that helps a group, or a couple, decide what to watch. The host creates a session and shares a QR code, link or code. Each person picks up to two vibes in under 90 seconds, then swipes 10 titles filtered to their streaming services and languages. The app shows the group's top 3, ranked by how many people liked each, and offers 10 more titles if nobody agrees. It needs no sign-up or download, works remotely, and has separate Friends and Couples pages.

questions: Why did he build Let's Match?
What problem does Let's Match solve?
entries.answer: Deciding what to watch takes longer with every extra person. Let's Match reduces that decision time by letting everyone react to the same small set of titles on their own phone, so the group's overlap shows up quickly instead of through negotiation.

entries.answer: Let's Match is live on its own domain and is currently in the testing phase. Many users are using it and sending constant feedback, but I don't have usage numbers to share. It is built on Next.js and was built with Claude Code. Title data comes from TMDB, where-to-watch data from JustWatch, and streaming availability from the Streaming Availability API by Movie of the Night.

questions: What did he build for marketing?
entries.answer: Performance AI is a prototype of a marketing decision product for performance marketers. The problem: marketers see spend, leads and CTR, but what matters is cost per revenue outcome, and the funnel leaks between lead and revenue. The product gives a daily brief of decisions needed, backed by diagnosis across the full funnel, campaign, city and platform, plus a forecast of cost per revenue outcome with a what-if. Guardrails set what the AI can act on, what goes to a review queue, and what is logged. It has five views (Brief, Diagnose, Forecast, Guardrails, Settings) and is shown for a fictional lender, Meridian Capital Finance, where the outcome is a loan disbursal.

questions: What did he build for customer operations?
entries.answer: Helix AI is a prototype of a Customer Experience OS for support teams. The problem: support leaders find SLA breaches, escalations and quality issues after the damage is done. Helix puts the work and the intelligence in one place, with Overview, Tickets, a Unified Inbox, Customers, AI Insights, Analytics, Agent Coaching, Automations, Team and Agents, and Settings, plus an Ask Helix assistant.

questions: What did he build for revenue operations?
entries.answer: Revora AI is a prototype of a billing and revenue operations product. The problem: revenue leaks quietly between contract, invoice, payment and collection, and finance finds it at month-end reconciliation, when recovery is hardest. Revora covers customers, subscriptions, invoicing, payments and collections, with a Revenue Leakage Monitor, AI Revenue Insights, workflows and approvals so a recommendation becomes an owned task. It has 16 modules, from Customers through Reconciliation to Settings.

questions: What did he build for compliance?
entries.answer: Comply is a prototype of a compliance operating layer for a fictional NBFC. The problem: regulatory change, controls and evidence live in different places, so nobody can quickly say which obligation, control and owner a new regulation affects. Comply provides one traceable chain from regulation to obligation to control to finding to remediation. It sits on top of existing tools (Vanta, Okta, AWS Config, Jira, Slack) instead of replacing them, requires every exception to carry an expiry and a compensating control, and shows whether evidence is current or stale. It has six modules: Command Centre, Regulatory Register, Controls and Ownership, Exceptions and Remediation, Audit Workspace, and Settings.

questions: What did he build for HR?
entries.answer: PeopleOS is a prototype of a skills-based talent intelligence product. The problem: HR systems store records, but decisions on hiring, mobility, development and succession depend on knowing who can do what. PeopleOS makes skills the thread across modules, with explainable skill matches, People Signals leaders can act on, and a Copilot for workforce questions. It has 20 views, including Employee 360, a Skills Intelligence heatmap, a Talent Marketplace, Succession and Workforce Planning.

questions: How does Prannav think about product?
How does he think about building products?
entries.answer: Two principles. Build, measure, iterate: strong product decisions combine structured thinking with real-world feedback, and the best way to learn what works is to build, measure the impact and keep improving. Value over interface: great products are defined by the value they deliver to the end user, combined with a user-friendly design, not by how good the interface looks.
